name: Ulimorelin
lead: Ulimorelin (TZP-101) is an investigational small-molecule ghrelin receptor agonist, developed by Tranzyme Pharma as a gut prokinetic.[1] Because it acts on the same receptor as the hunger hormone ghrelin, people interested in appetite and body weight discuss it as a peripherally acting ghrelin agonist, with the appearance link running through appetite and digestive function in people who want to gain or keep weight.

It is a macrocyclic peptidomimetic found by screening Tranzyme's macrocycle library against the human ghrelin receptor and then optimised for pharmacokinetics.[1][2] It was given intravenously in early trials for postoperative ileus and diabetic gastroparesis, where phase 2 results were encouraging.[3][4]

Two phase 3 trials (ULISES 007 and 008) tested daily infusions after partial bowel resection.[5] A later phase 2 trial compared it with metoclopramide in 120 critically ill patients with enteral feeding intolerance.[6] It has not been approved as a medicine.

angle.text: Ulimorelin is discussed as a ghrelin-pathway compound that increases gut motility rather than a growth hormone booster. People interested in gaining or maintaining weight follow it for its link to feeding tolerance.

infobox: Postoperative ileus, gastroparesis, enteral feeding intolerance

paras: Tranzyme's high-throughput screen against the ghrelin receptor produced macrocyclic hits that were potent but had poor pharmacokinetics; medicinal chemistry work led to ulimorelin.[2]

A phase 2 trial in 267 patients after major open abdominal surgery and a phase 2 gastroparesis trial in 78 patients were run in 2007.[7][8] In severe diabetic gastroparesis, a subset analysis reported relief of symptoms with nausea and vomiting.[4] A covariate analysis found faster gut recovery independent of opioid use and surgery type.[3]

In the phase 3 ULISES programme, patients received 30-minute infusions after surgery, and the main outcome was time to first bowel movement and tolerance of solid food.[5] A Phase 1 study later concluded that once-daily dosing may have missed the colon, which recovers last, and showed that 8-hourly dosing produced sustained gastric emptying gains of 23% to 46%.[9]
In the PROMOTE trial, 120 ICU patients were randomised to ulimorelin or metoclopramide for 5 days; the drugs gave comparable feeding results.[6]
Studies in rats found that ulimorelin lowers blood pressure through a mechanism not dependent on the classic ghrelin receptor.[10][11]

timeline.event: Phase 2 trials of TZP-101 begin in postoperative ileus and diabetic gastroparesis.[7][8]
Phase 3 ULISES 007 and 008 trials start; medicinal chemistry paper published.[2][5]
PROMOTE trial in ICU patients with enteral feeding intolerance begins.[12]
Phase 1 study of dosing, gastric emptying and colonic transit published.[9]

card.summary: An investigational gut-acting ghrelin receptor agonist, tested to speed digestion and feeding, followed by people interested in appetite and weight.
card.note: Investigational; given by IV in trials and not approved.

quick.overview:
Ulimorelin (TZP-101) is a ghrelin receptor agonist built to speed movement through the gut. It was tested in post-surgery bowel recovery, gastroparesis and ICU feeding problems.

People interested in appetite and weight follow it as a ghrelin-pathway compound that acts mainly on digestion.
quick.mechanism: It activates the ghrelin receptor on gut nerves and muscle, which increases gastric emptying and colonic motility. Dosing frequency mattered in trials, since once-daily dosing did not sustain the effect.
quick.risks: Trials reported it as generally well tolerated, though phase 3 postoperative ileus studies did not meet expectations and it is not approved. Rat studies show a blood-pressure-lowering effect through a separate mechanism.
